notes:
I mapped all 315 names (n 2100–2414). Things to check:

1) Thrush names. 'Thrush' (274 observations) and 'Thrushes' (974) are set to Song Thrush as you asked. In reports of big night movements, 'Thrushes' may also cover Redwing and Fieldfare, so a sample check is worth it given the size. Turdus musicus is set to Song Thrush because that was the 1880s usage, and the same lists name Redwing separately as iliacus.

2) Family headings garbled by OCR (Turpipz, Turpip#, Torpip#, Twrdide, Turdide, Turdidez) are all set to Turdidae. In the 1880s Turdidae also included chats, robins and wheatears, which are now in Muscicapidae.

3) The 'TROGLODYTIDÆ' and 'TROGLODYTINS' headings are mapped to the species Eurasian Wren, because it is the only British member. Make sure nothing else is filed under them.

4) Victorian genus names don't match the modern ones:
   - Tringa then meant the stints, Dunlin and Knot (now Calidris), so I gave genus Calidris.
   - Totanus then meant the shanks plus Common Sandpiper, so I gave genus Tringa.

5) Possible rarities to check for locality and plausibility: American Robin, White's Thrush (Turdus varius and 'White Thrush'), Citrine Wagtail, Brünnich's Guillemot (Thick-billed Murre), Pectoral Sandpiper, Wilson's Storm Petrel (these may be misidentified storm petrels), and Yellow-barred Warbler (probably Yellow-browed). A 'Wood Wren' on 27 October is very late for Wood Warbler.

6) Mixed or ambiguous names:
   - 'White Owl': the book name was Barn Owl, but the example's 'great White Owl' at Redcar reads like Snowy Owl. I gave group 'owls'; check both observations.
   - 'White Kittiwake' and 'white Sea Gull of the Kittiwake variety' may be Ivory Gulls.
   - 'White and Blue Throats' is two species in one name; it should probably be split.
   - 'young Curlew' records in May are probably Whimbrels.
   - The quoted 'Grey' Plover may be Golden Plover.

7) Left unknown: White-Breast and Whitebreast, White-backed (alone), white-bellied variety, Winter Sparrows, Willy the Wisp, 'Bass' Gulls, Welw Bail, Wihiehae, and the references back to earlier text (these birds, the common species). Most of these can be settled from the surrounding text.

8) Conventions I chose:
   - 'Wild Duck' is family Anatidae, not Mallard.
   - 'Water Wagtail' is White Wagtail (Pied).
   - Tit and Tomtit names are family Paridae. The Titmouses said to breed on the Rock may be Rock Pipits.
   - 'Wagtail(s)' is genus Motacilla.
   - 'Woodguests' is Wood Pigeon (Scots 'woodquest').
   - 'Wen', 'ween' and 'Uarks' are read as Wren, Wren and Larks.

9) IOC names you may want to override with British ones: Common Murre (Guillemot), Western House Martin, Western Yellow Wagtail, Eurasian Whimbrel and Curruca communis (Whitethroat).
